analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from discriminating against workers because they care for family members.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in late November 2022 with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for employers to refuse to hire, fire, cut pay, change schedules, or otherwise punish workers because they help support or care for a family member. It would be enforced by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and through private lawsuits, with penalties funding grants to educate workers and employers about the new rights. It also covers gig and contract workers, no matter how they are labeled.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of workers who help support or care for a spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, or even a close family-equivalent relationship — including contract and gig workers. They could keep their jobs, pay, and schedules without being penalized for caregiving, and could sue directly in court without first filing an agency complaint.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to refuse to hire, fire, harass, or discriminate against an applicant or employee in pay, advancement, scheduling, or other terms of employment because of family caregiver responsibilities, defined broadly to cover anyone responsible for supporting or caring for a family member of any age [S3].

It creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation if an employer takes adverse action against a worker within two years of the worker asserting these rights, and protects even mistaken but good-faith complaints [S3].
It lets workers sue directly in court without first filing a charge with the EEOC or exhausting administrative remedies, a faster route than most discrimination claims allow [S3].

It covers independent contractors regardless of the label an employer uses, closing a common loophole, and also prohibits employers from threatening workers with immigration reporting in retaliation for asserting these rights [S3].

Penalties — up to $10,000 per discrimination violation and $5,000 per retaliation violation — would go into a fund for grants to nonprofit and academic groups that educate workers and employers and support workers facing caregiver discrimination [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, including companies that use independent contractors, bear the cost of potential lawsuits, penalties, workplace notices, and changed hiring and scheduling decisions. Some employers argue caregiving-based rules create litigation risk and make them more cautious about hiring workers who may need flexibility.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets workers skip the EEOC charge process entirely and sue directly, and it presumes retaliation for any adverse action within two years of a complaint unless the employer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence — a burden higher than in ordinary civil cases — which could expose employers to costly litigation over legitimate personnel decisions [S3].

The definitions are broad: 'family member' includes relatives by blood or affinity 'equivalent of a family relationship,' and the covered responsibility includes merely being regarded as a contributor to a family member's support, which employers could argue is vague enough to invite disputes over ordinary scheduling and staffing decisions [S3].

Because enforcement mirrors Title VII but adds a private right of action without administrative exhaustion, small businesses in particular could face compliance and legal costs alongside the required workplace notices, with fines for posting violations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection fills a real gap: federal law protects workers against race, sex, disability, and pregnancy discrimination, but a worker who is passed over or pushed out because they care for an aging parent or a sick child generally has no federal claim. The main cost falls on employers as litigation exposure and compliance work, and the bill's broad definitions and strong retaliation presumption — including a two-year presumption and a clear-and-convincing rebuttal standard — go beyond comparable state laws, so some of the criticism about overbreadth is fair. On balance, the protection is meaningful for a large group of workers, though the bill never advanced far enough for its design details to be tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on November 29, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the same day; that was the bill's final action in the record [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it to the floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who might have faced caregiver-discrimination liability avoided a new set of legal obligations, and no worker gained new protections because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoided new liability; workers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and issued it to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, which relied on no Republican support in the Senate that had 50 Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party — no Republican signed on, and no other Democrat did either in the weeks before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would have created a new federal discrimination claim, penalties, and a private right of action against employers who penalize caregiving. The bill's death leaves workers without that protection and employers without new liability.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and staffing firms using contractors
industries.note: The bill would have covered independent contractors regardless of how they were classified, removing a label-based shield from caregiver-discrimination claims. Because the bill died, that exposure never arrived.

New anti-discrimination claims generate work for plaintiff-side lawyers, HR consultants, and compliance training providers, but the bill would also have funded nonprofit education and support for affected workers. With no law, neither happened.
